5.1 — The Axe: Item Pickups & Inventory Bools

Coins and potions changed numbers. The axe changes what you are: it flips a boolean, swaps your entire animation set, and suddenly you look like someone who can break down a door. Today you build a pickup that grants capability instead of a count — and you discover that changing a weapon is not a transition you draw, it is a controller you replace.

Predict First ~10 min

Before you build anything, answer the data question. Coins needed a counter. A potion needed to change an existing number. What does "the player is carrying an axe" actually need?

OptionWhat it storesWhy you would or would not
An int count How many axes you hold Useless extra information. Nobody has ever needed two axes. You would be storing a number you will never read.
A bool Yes or no — you have one, or you do not The honest shape of the fact. One item, one yes/no.
A list of items Every item you carry, by name The right answer for sixty items. Overkill for one, and it makes the simplest question — "do I have an axe?" — into a search.

Socratic: Right-sizing the data

  1. Why is a bool the right abstraction for "I have an axe" but the wrong one for "how many coins do I have"?
  2. At roughly how many items does a collection of booleans become the wrong design? What breaks first — readability, or the number of branches you have to write?
  3. Where should this boolean live — on the axe, on the player, or somewhere global? Use the reasoning you applied in 2.1, then check it against what you actually do below.
  4. You already store coins and health on PlayerController. Is "has an axe" the same kind of fact? What makes it different from a number, if anything?
Build Lab: The pickup ~25 min

Step 1 — put an axe in the world. Open Assets/Prefabs/AxeItem and read its Inspector. Then answer this before touching anything: if you walked into this object right now, would anything happen?

Architectural specification: making it a pickup.
  • The prefab carries the tag Axe already. What is it missing that every other pickup in this game has? Add it, and choose trigger or solid with a reason.
  • There are currently zero axes placed in any scene. Drag an instance into the Overworld somewhere your player will find it. How will you know the tester can reach it?
  • Where does the "I have an axe" field live? What type, what default value, and why must the default be what it is rather than the opposite?
  • Which callback receives the pickup, and how do you confirm the thing you touched is the axe rather than a coin? (You have written this check twice already.)
  • Should collecting the axe destroy it? Compare against the coin from 2.1 and the potion from 2.3 — is the axe the same kind of object?

Notice what this pickup does not do: it changes no number and prints no count. The axe is a permission — a fact that future code will read before allowing an action. You are not building a score, you are building a capability.

Step 2 — prove it is real state. Add a temporary Debug.Log that prints the boolean every frame. Run the game: watch the Console repeat the default value, walk into the axe, and watch it flip. Then delete the print — the proof is the behaviour, not the message.

Step 3 — the interesting part: change how the player looks. Open the Player's Animator and read which controller it is using. Now go and look at Assets/Artwork/Animations/Top_Down/PlayerAnimator/ and see what else is in that folder. You will find a second, complete controller — axe swings instead of shovel swings — and it is not assigned to anything. Someone built you the whole weapon set and left it on the shelf.

Socratic: Three ways to change a weapon

All three of these are legitimate. Read the cost column before you commit:

ApproachHow it worksWhat it costs
Assign the other controller at runtime The Animator component has a property holding the controller it is currently using. Set it to the axe controller when the axe is picked up, and the whole state machine — states, transitions, clips — is replaced instantly. Nothing to author. You must remember to set it back if the axe is ever lost.
Author the axe states into one controller Add the axe states and transitions into the controller you already have, and drive them with a new parameter. You duplicate an entire state machine by hand, and every future clip must be added twice.
Use an Animator Override Controller A Unity asset built for exactly this: it takes one base controller and swaps the clips it plays, keeping all the logic in one place. One extra asset to create, and one more concept to learn. This is the professional answer.
  1. Which approach does the project's own art layout clearly intend you to take? What is the evidence?
  2. Read Assets/Scripts/Package Scripts/SceneSwitch.cs. Find where it saves and restores something related to the Animator. Which property does it touch, and what does that prove is possible at runtime?
  3. Which approach would you choose if this game had four weapons instead of two, and why does the answer change?
  4. What is the name of the property on the Animator component that holds the controller? Find it in the documentation rather than guessing.

Build the version you chose, then walk into the axe and swing. If you took the first approach, your character should visibly become someone else the moment you touch it.

Bug Hunt: The phantom axe

  1. Set the boolean's starting value to the "already has it" state. What does the game grant you before you ever found the axe — and what did the default you originally chose protect against?
  2. Pick up the axe, then die using the death rule you built in 2.2. Do you still have the axe? Should you — and is that a coding decision or a design decision?
  3. Add a second axe and collect both. What does the boolean become after the second one? Why is that the only correct answer even though you touched two axes?
  4. If you took the runtime-swap approach, what happens to the player's appearance when a scene loads? Check what SceneSwitch.cs does about it, and explain why that code has to exist.
  5. Change the name your code uses for an Animator parameter so it no longer matches the controller. What is the symptom — silence, an error, or nothing at all? What does that tell you about the cost of string-based APIs?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Inventory design

  1. Look in Assets/Character/Player/ExtraSpriteSheets/. How many alternative weapon sets ship with this project? What would each one cost you to wire up, under the approach you chose?
  2. Design the feedback: how would a player see that they are holding an axe? Argue sprite-only versus a UI icon — and which does the animation swap give you for free?
  3. The one-use axe: breaking the door consumes it, so the boolean flips back to false. Which script should flip it back, and why must it not be the pickup branch that does so?
  4. Right now your boolean is lost when the scene reloads. Write down exactly what that means for the player. You will fix this in 5.3, and the fix will not be about the axe.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain when a bool fits a fact and when it does not, and right-size the data for a new pickup
  • Build an item that grants capability instead of changing a number
  • Compare the three ways to change a weapon set, and defend your choice
  • Find a property in the Unity documentation rather than guessing its name
  • Explain what SceneSwitch.cs does about the Animator, and why it must
  • Commit and push
